pages.text: On the teacher’s table stood three glass jars. One held muddy water from a pond, one held water from a borehole, and one held water from a tap. “Look and smell carefully, but never taste any of these samples,” said the teacher. “Good drinking water is clear, has no bad smell, and has no germs.”
sentences: On the teacher’s table stood three glass jars.
One held muddy water from a pond, one held water from a borehole, and one held water from a tap.
“Look and smell carefully, but never taste any of these samples,” said the teacher.
“Good drinking water is clear, has no bad smell, and has no germs.”
pages.alt: In a Ghanaian classroom, Brobbey and Amegashie inspect three unlabelled glass jars of muddy, borehole, and tap water on their teacher’s table.

pages.text: Together, the class built a simple filter. Earlier, the teacher had safely cut a plastic bottle and turned the top half upside down like a funnel, layering clean cloth, sand, and small washed stones inside. When Brobbey poured in the muddy water, the water that dripped out below was much clearer.
sentences: Together, the class built a simple filter.
Earlier, the teacher had safely cut a plastic bottle and turned the top half upside down like a funnel, layering clean cloth, sand, and small washed stones inside.
When Brobbey poured in the muddy water, the water that dripped out below was much clearer.
pages.alt: Brobbey pours muddy water into an inverted plastic bottle filter layered with cloth, sand, and small pebbles as clearer water drips into a jar below.

pages.text: “Is it safe to drink now?” asked Amegashie thoughtfully. “No,” said the teacher. “Clear water can still hold germs, and germs are far too small for our eyes to see. Filtering only takes out dirt. We must also kill the germs.”
sentences: “Is it safe to drink now?” asked Amegashie thoughtfully.
“No,” said the teacher.
“Clear water can still hold germs, and germs are far too small for our eyes to see.
Filtering only takes out dirt.
We must also kill the germs.”
pages.alt: Amegashie looks thoughtfully at the jar of clearer filtered water while her teacher holds up a gentle warning finger.

pages.text: “One sure way is boiling,” said the teacher. “Boiling water for a few minutes and letting it cool in a clean, covered container kills germs and makes it safe to drink. Remember, children must never boil water alone or touch hot pots; a grown-up must do it.”
sentences: “One sure way is boiling,” said the teacher.
“Boiling water for a few minutes and letting it cool in a clean, covered container kills germs and makes it safe to drink.
Remember, children must never boil water alone or touch hot pots; a grown-up must do it.”
pages.alt: The teacher points to a wordless classroom picture showing an adult safely boiling water in a covered pot on a stove as Brobbey and Amegashie listen.

pages.text: “Another way is to use safe chlorine drops or a water-treatment tablet,” he explained. “An adult must follow the health worker’s instructions for the exact amount. Alum helps mud settle to the bottom, but alum alone does not kill germs.”
sentences: “Another way is to use safe chlorine drops or a water-treatment tablet,” he explained.
“An adult must follow the health worker’s instructions for the exact amount.
Alum helps mud settle to the bottom, but alum alone does not kill germs.”
pages.alt: The teacher holds up a plain unlabelled blister strip of water-treatment tablets beside a covered clay water pot while Brobbey and Amegashie watch.

pages.text: The class drew a five-step picture chart: filter, boil, treat, cover, and store cleanly. Then they discussed the dangers of unsafe water. “Unclean water can cause serious stomach illnesses,” said Brobbey. “So we must make drinking water safe and always keep it covered!”

Then they discussed the dangers of unsafe water.
“Unclean water can cause serious stomach illnesses,” said Brobbey.
“So we must make drinking water safe and always keep it covered!”
pages.alt: Brobbey, Amegashie, and classmates proudly hold up a wordless five-panel picture poster showing filtering, boiling, water drops, and a covered pot.

activities.question: Why is clear water not always safe to drink?
options: It can still hold germs too small to see

activities.question: Who should boil water or handle water-treatment chemicals?

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making muddy water safe in order.
items: Filter out the mud and dirt.
A grown-up boils the clear water.
Store it in a clean, covered container.

A spoon that stirs sugar into tea

glossary.definition: A tool that traps dirt as water passes through.
Tiny living things too small to see that can cause illness.
Heating water until bubbles rise briskly, which kills germs.
A safe water-treatment chemical that kills germs when used in the right amount.
